text:
The Day “They” Disappeared

Part One

At 5:17 on a Tuesday morning, America changed.

There was no explosion. There was no emergency broadcast. There were no sirens. There was no announcement from Washington telling people what had happened or what they were supposed to do next.

Millions of people were simply gone.

Sometime between midnight and sunrise, every person living in the United States without legal immigration status disappeared.

Just disappeared.

Their beds were empty. Their cars were still sitting in apartment parking lots and driveways. Coffee cups were sitting beside kitchen sinks. Cell phones were plugged into chargers. Work boots were waiting beside front doors. Lunches packed the night before were sitting inside refrigerators. Some televisions were still playing. Some alarm clocks started ringing in empty bedrooms.

And America woke up.

At first, almost nobody understood what had happened.

There was no national moment of realization. It happened one person at a time.

A husband rolled over and discovered his wife was gone. A child walked into her mother’s bedroom and found an empty bed. A restaurant manager started calling employees who never answered. A farmer looked across an empty parking lot. A construction superintendent stood at the entrance to a job site wondering where everybody was.

Millions of individual moments of confusion were happening at exactly the same time.

In Yuma, Arizona, a farm supervisor named Rick Martinez pulled into work before sunrise. He had probably made that same drive hundreds of times. But the moment he entered the employee parking lot, he knew something was wrong.

Normally there were dozens of cars.

That morning there were seven.

Seven.

Rick sat behind the steering wheel for a few seconds, staring through the windshield.

Maybe he had gotten the schedule wrong. Maybe something had happened on the highway. Maybe there had been some sort of misunderstanding.

He walked into the break room.

Three workers were sitting inside.

“Where is everybody?”

Nobody knew.

Phones started coming out. Calls were made. Voicemails were left.

Nobody answered.

By 7:00 that morning, Rick had 180 acres scheduled for harvest and almost nobody there to harvest them.

Now here is the problem.

Vegetables do not care about immigration policy. They do not care who won the election. They do not care what somebody promised during a campaign. They do not care what somebody shouted at a rally. They do not care whether you watch Fox News, CNN, MSNBC, or nothing at all.

They are ready when they are ready.

Today the crop was ready. Tomorrow some of it would already begin deteriorating. A few days after that, much of it would be worthless.

Rick started calling every labor contractor he knew.

The strange thing was, they were calling him too.

Everybody was asking the same question.

Where is everybody?

By noon, farmers throughout Arizona, California, Texas, Florida, Washington, and dozens of other states were discovering the same thing.

The people were gone.

The crops were still there.

And the clock was already running.

Over in Scottsdale, a construction superintendent named Tom Bradley was dealing with a completely different version of the same problem.

Tom was supervising construction of a luxury apartment complex scheduled to open in six weeks. Normally, more than one hundred workers showed up every morning.

That morning, thirty-nine arrived.

Thirty-nine.

The drywall crews were missing. Roofers were missing. Concrete workers were missing. Landscaping crews were missing. Painters were missing.

Several subcontractors stopped answering their phones completely because they no longer had enough employees to operate.

Tom walked around the construction site, looking at unfinished walls, exposed wiring, stacks of drywall, concrete forms, pallets of tile, and millions of dollars worth of equipment.

Everything was there.

Except the people.

Eventually, Tom called the developer.

“We are not opening in six weeks.”

There was silence on the other end.

“How long?”

Tom looked across the construction site. For the first time that morning, he understood that this was not going to be fixed tomorrow.

“I have no idea.”

Across town, a restaurant owner named Michelle unlocked her kitchen door at 8:30.

Her dishwasher was gone. Two cooks were gone. One busser was gone. The overnight cleaning crew had never arrived.

One of her servers came in crying because her husband had disappeared sometime during the night. Another employee never showed up because she was trying to figure out what had happened to her mother.

Technically, Michelle had enough employees to unlock the front door.

She did not have enough employees to actually run the restaurant.

So the owner started washing dishes.

By lunch, she closed half the dining room. Customers complained about the wait. Some complained loudly.

They had no idea what was happening.

By dinner, Michelle had had enough.

She closed the restaurant.

She wrote two sentences on a piece of paper and taped it to the front door.

STAFF SHORTAGE.

PLEASE BE PATIENT.

Similar signs began appearing everywhere.

Restaurants. Hotels. Construction companies. Landscaping companies. Car washes. Cleaning companies. Warehouses. Food processing plants. Agricultural operations.

By the end of the first day, Americans were beginning to realize something had happened.

By the second day, they were beginning to understand how big it was.

And by the third day, they were starting to feel it.

People began noticing the grocery stores.

At first, it was subtle.

The produce section looked a little thinner. A few empty spaces appeared where tomatoes normally sat. Then lettuce. Then strawberries. Then certain fruits and vegetables disappeared completely.

The meat department started looking different. Then dairy. Then packaged foods.

It was not because America had suddenly run out of food.

There was food everywhere.

There were vegetables sitting in fields. There were cattle. There were chickens. There were warehouses filled with products.

But that really was not the issue.

The issue was everything that had to happen before food ended up in your shopping cart.

Somebody had to harvest it. Somebody had to process it. Somebody had to package it. Somebody had to clean the facility. Somebody had to move the pallets. Somebody had to load the truck. Somebody had to unload the truck. Somebody had to stock the shelf.

Remove enough people from enough points in that system, and suddenly the whole thing begins slowing down.

That is when America started discovering something that most of us rarely think about.

Our economy is not a bunch of separate businesses operating independently.

It is a web.

Every job connects to another job. Every industry connects to another industry. Every worker depends upon somebody else doing something somewhere.

Pull millions of people out of that web overnight, and strands begin snapping in places nobody expected.

Three days after the disappearance, tomatoes were selling for nearly twice what they had cost the week before in some cities.

Restaurants started increasing prices. Hotels reduced housekeeping. Landscaping companies canceled appointments. Roofing contractors pushed projects back for months. Construction schedules began collapsing. Some meat processing facilities reduced production. Factories shortened shifts. Warehouses struggled to fill orders.

Produce began rotting in fields while grocery stores hundreds of miles away had empty spaces on shelves.

And suddenly, Americans were learning something that had always been true.

Labor has value.

There were winners.

At least at first.

In Phoenix, a twenty-three-year-old man named Jason Walker had been looking for construction work.

Before Tuesday, Jason had been calling employers.

Now employers were calling Jason.

One contractor offered him $24 an hour. Another offered $27. A roofing company offered $30.

Jason took the $30.

And good for Jason.

Workers like him suddenly had leverage. Employers who had spent years saying Americans would not take these jobs were discovering something.

Some Americans absolutely would do them.

For enough money.

But there was another side to that.

The roofing company was suddenly paying thousands of dollars more every week in labor. That money had to come from somewhere.

It came from the customer.

The price of replacing a roof went up. The cost of building a house went up. Restaurants increased prices. Hotels increased prices. Construction companies increased prices. Farmers increased prices.

Consumers paid the difference.

But something much darker was happening away from the farms, restaurants, construction sites, and grocery stores.

It was happening inside American homes.

Nine-year-old Sofia Hernandez woke up in Denver and walked into her parents’ bedroom.

Her father was sitting on the edge of the bed.

Her mother was gone.

At first, Sofia thought her mother had gone to work early. Then she noticed her mother’s purse. Her shoes. Her phone. Her wedding ring sitting beside the bed.

Her father was an American citizen. Sofia was an American citizen.

Her mother had lived in the United States for sixteen years without legal status.

She had kissed her daughter goodnight Monday evening.

Tuesday morning, she was gone.

There had been no goodbye. No suitcase packed. No final conversation. No final hug. No chance for Sofia to understand what was happening.

One evening, she had a mother.

The next morning, she did not.

And Sofia was not alone.

Millions of Americans were discovering something our political arguments rarely acknowledge.

Immigration status does not divide families into nice, clean categories.

Citizen children have undocumented parents. Legal residents have undocumented spouses. American citizens have undocumented brothers, sisters, friends, coworkers, employees, neighbors, church members, and people they love.

Suddenly, this was not simply an immigration story.

It was not simply an economic story.

It was a human story.

Schools began reporting thousands of children absent. Some children had lost a parent. Some had lost both. Some parents had suddenly become single parents.

Teachers found children crying at their desks. Counselors were overwhelmed. Churches opened their doors. Food drives began. Teachers collected clothing. Businesses created emergency funds. Neighbors started taking care of children whose families had been torn apart overnight.

And then the nursing homes started calling.

So did home health companies.

They had lost workers too.

People who had quietly spent years caring for elderly Americans were suddenly gone.

The people who changed bedsheets, prepared meals, cleaned rooms, lifted patients, changed diapers, helped people use bathrooms, administered routine care, and held the hands of frightened old people at three in the morning when nobody else was there.

Gone.

Families started receiving phone calls.

“We need you to come get your mother.”

“We don’t have enough staff.”

“We cannot maintain normal operations.”

“We are sorry.”

Imagine getting that call.

Now imagine getting it when you have a job, children, a mortgage, and absolutely no idea how you are supposed to become a full-time caregiver tomorrow morning.

For years, America had argued about undocumented immigration using numbers.

Ten million. Fifteen million. Twenty million.

People argued about which number was correct.

Suddenly, the number did not matter very much.

Because numbers had become empty chairs. Numbers had become unfinished houses. Numbers had become rotting crops. Numbers had become closed restaurants. Numbers had become frightened elderly people. Numbers had become children staring into empty bedrooms.

By the second week, Washington was in chaos.

Some politicians who had spent years promising mass removals appeared on television declaring victory.

The undocumented population was gone.

Problem solved.

Except something strange was happening on the television screen right beside them.

Fields of vegetables were rotting. Construction sites were sitting silent. Restaurants were closed. Farmers were begging for workers. Restaurant associations were demanding emergency visas. Construction companies wanted expanded legal immigration. Agricultural organizations wanted temporary labor programs expanded immediately.

Economists argued about inflation. Politicians shouted at one another. Everybody blamed somebody else.

And some Americans asked what I think is actually a perfectly reasonable question.

Why were American businesses depending upon people who were living here illegally in the first place?

Fair question.

We absolutely should ask it.

But then we have to be willing to ask the next question too.

Why did we allow it?

For decades, America created an incredible contradiction.

We demanded strict immigration enforcement.

But we also demanded inexpensive food, cheap construction, affordable landscaping, fast restaurant service, affordable hotel rooms, low-cost produce, home health care, meat processing, roofing, cleaning, and agricultural labor.

We wanted everything the labor produced.

We liked the prices that labor helped make possible.

We liked having somebody clean the hotel room. We liked having somebody pick the strawberries. We liked having somebody put a new roof on the house in July. We liked having somebody take care of Mom when she could no longer take care of herself.

We just did not spend very much time wondering who those people were.

Or where they came from.

Or whether they went home to American children at night.

For years, we talked about them as if they were something separate from us.

“They.”

Those people.

Illegal immigrants.

A statistic.

A problem to be solved.

And then one Tuesday morning, “they” disappeared.

By the end of the first week, something uncomfortable was becoming obvious.

“They” had never really been separate from America at all.

They had been standing beside us the entire time.

Working beside us. Living beside us. Worshipping beside us. Buying groceries beside us. Raising children beside us. Building our houses. Harvesting our food. Cleaning our businesses. Caring for our parents.

And now they were gone.

America had spent decades asking what would happen if we could somehow make all of them disappear.

Now we knew.

And this was only the first week. https://t.co/h0uoLI8Wx2

Why move that truck line now

•  Texas already has the truck campus. San Antonio already builds the Tundra and Sequoia. Adding Tacoma there creates one big U.S. truck/SUV hub, with a new axle plant and room to grow. Texas also offered incentives. ￼

•  Tacoma sells huge numbers in the U.S. It is too important a product to leave fully exposed to border tariffs and trade fights.

text:
The History of how Curry travelled to Japan! 🇯🇵 But First…

When I first saw this episode on ‘One Piece’, I had no idea it was a reference to REAL life. Apparently, the Japanese Navy really does eat curry every Friday!

Every Friday, on every Japanese navy ship at sea, the crew eats curry. Ask why, and you'll usually hear it’s so sailors don't lose track of what day it is out on the water. That's only half of the reason.

The real answer starts a century and a half earlier when Japan had just decided to model its naval development against Britain’s navy down to the last detail.

What British sailors ate, on long voyages, was curry. The British had picked it up in India, through the East India Company, and remade it into something more to their own taste: meat and vegetables in a thick, flour-based sauce, built around a spice blend sold ready-made as "curry powder." It was hearty, it traveled, and a ship's cook could make a huge batch of it without much skill. The British Royal Navy had been feeding it to sailors for years before Japan came looking for a navy to model after. 

You might wonder, but WHY did the Sailors eat Curry?

𝗕𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗸𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗠𝗼𝗻𝗼𝘁𝗼𝗻𝘆 𝗼𝗳 𝗦𝗮𝗹𝘁𝗲𝗱 𝗠𝗲𝗮𝘁𝘀: Naval rations consisted of hardtack (biscuits) and heavily salted beef or pork preserved in barrels. This meat was incredibly dry, intensely salty, and very monotonous. Curry powder provided a cheap, highly flavorful variety that broke up the bleak boredom of daily seafaring rations.

𝗣𝗿𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 "𝗕𝗲𝗿𝗶𝗯𝗲𝗿𝗶" 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗠𝗮𝗹𝗻𝘂𝘁𝗿𝗶𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻: Long voyages meant restricted diets and severe nutrient deficiencies. The curry that the Sailors ate was a thick stew loaded with root vegetables, meat, and a sauce thickened with wheat flour. San Francisco is trying something different on homelessness. Seattle should be watching
September 21, 2026
San Francisco is trying something different on homelessness. Seattle should be watching

Seattle and San Francisco have wrestled with many of the same problems for years: tents on sidewalks, open-air drug use, untreated mental illness, and enormous public spending that has too often failed to produce the progress residents were promised.

But today, the two cities are moving in noticeably different directions.

In San Francisco, Mayor Daniel Lurie has made addiction and mental health central to his homelessness strategy. His “Breaking the Cycle” initiative explicitly links shelter with treatment, behavioral-health care, recovery housing, street outreach, enforcement, and greater accountability for the organizations receiving public money.

The goal is not simply to find someone a bed for the night. San Francisco is trying to create different places for people with different needs.

That has included hundreds of new stabilization, treatment, and recovery beds, including drug- and alcohol-free transitional housing. By April 2026, San Francisco’s Department of Public Health said it had added more than 200 behavioral-health residential treatment and care beds and converted another 100, including withdrawal-management beds, recovery housing, and a 24-hour crisis stabilization center for people experiencing serious mental-health or substance-use crises.

Lurie has also reorganized the city’s street response. Instead of a collection of separate outreach programs operating alongside police and other agencies, San Francisco moved toward neighborhood teams coordinating public health, homelessness services, police, fire, the sheriff, public works, and emergency management. The purpose is to connect people with appropriate services while also responding to encampments, public drug use, and other street conditions.

And this year, Lurie advanced the RESET Center, which is designed to take people arrested for public intoxication to a staffed stabilization facility rather than simply cycling them through jail or a hospital emergency room. Once there, they can be evaluated, stabilized, and connected with treatment.

Former Seattle Mayor Tim Burgess recently argued in Post Alley that the changes are significant enough that Seattle should be paying attention. He pointed to fewer encampments, falling crime, expanded shelter, and Lurie’s willingness to experiment with treatment and recovery models that go beyond a predominantly low-barrier approach.

Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson started the year with a different emphasis.

Wilson acknowledged in February that Seattle’s existing homelessness response had not produced acceptable results and made rapidly expanding emergency shelter one of her administration’s biggest priorities. She initially promised 1,000 new units of shelter or emergency housing in 2026, part of a broader campaign pledge to add roughly 4,000 during her term. Tiny-house villages were a significant piece of that strategy.

Now that promise has been substantially scaled back.

Wilson’s newly released plan calls for about 960 additional shelter beds by the end of 2027, rather than 1,000 each year. The mayor has cited the city’s roughly $175 million budget deficit and the practical difficulty of bringing that much capacity online as reasons for the change.

The administration says several new shelters will include specialized mental-health care, medical services, and substance-use treatment. It also proposes roughly $11.2 million next year for rental assistance, eviction prevention, case management, and related programs intended to keep people from becoming homeless in the first place.

What Seattle still does not have is a direct equivalent to Lurie’s broader framework.

San Francisco has put treatment capacity, recovery-focused housing, crisis stabilization, coordinated street intervention, public drug-use enforcement, and measurable provider outcomes under the same homelessness and behavioral-health strategy. Seattle’s approach remains heavily anchored to Housing First, which has never generated results commensurate with its costs.

That choice is becoming more consequential as Seattle and King County also restructure the King County Regional Homelessness Authority, bringing many contracts and spending decisions back under direct city and county control. It gives local leaders another opportunity to decide not simply how much to spend, but what outcomes taxpayers should expect from that spending.

San Francisco’s experience does not prove that every element of Lurie’s model would work the same way in Seattle. The cities have different governments, housing markets, service systems, and street populations, and San Francisco still faces serious homelessness and addiction problems of its own.

But it does provide a current example of a major West Coast city treating homelessness, addiction, and serious mental illness as interconnected problems rather than separate policy areas.

The contrast with San Francisco also comes as questions about Wilson’s leadership extend well beyond homelessness. Her administration has faced criticism over public safety, its response to the deadly Bite of Seattle shooting, and now whether the city has a clear path forward on one of its most persistent crises.

Those concerns led Change Washington to launch a petition calling for Wilson to resign as mayor. The petition, which is not a recall and carries no legal force, cites homelessness and drug use among a broader set of concerns about the direction of the city.

The response has been incredible, with more than a thousand people signing on already and offering comments. Paula C., for example, writes, “When you’re responsible for a city this important, the mayor’s office should not be where you learn how to run one. Seattle is paying too high a price for on-the-job training.”

And Margo H. said, “I have been horrified at her lack of adult behavior, her inability to communicate and have anything meaningful to say (other than a prearranged script) and blaming others, instead of admitting she is out of her league.”

Please continue to share the petition with friends and family.
https://t.co/UVXptmD3VV

The petition aside, Wilson still has an opportunity to show what her administration intends to do differently. San Francisco offers one example of a city putting addiction treatment, mental health care, recovery, and accountability more squarely into its homelessness response. For Seattle residents, the question now is whether Wilson will pursue a comparably clear strategy, and what they should conclude about her leadership if she does not.

text:
YEMEN, THE LAND OF ANSAR ALLAH!

GEOGRAPHY HAS CHECKMATED RIYADH

Saudi Arabia sits inside a box it cannot bomb its way out of. 
🇾🇪 Ansar Allah holds the southern rim of that box. Mountain ranges, Red Sea approaches, and the narrow Bab al-Mandeb give the movement reach without the burden of occupying every Saudi city.

Riyadh’s planners still talk as if air power can erase a neighbor that already proved, over a decade of war, that occupation of Yemen is a grave, not a strategy. The map does not care about palace talking points.

ANSAR ALLAH ADVANCES WHILE PACTS CRUMBLE

The Jerusalem Post itself describes a zugzwang: Houthis press forward while the alliances Riyadh assembled fail to cover the kingdom’s actual security holes. 
🇾🇪 That is not a media flourish. It is an admission that the campaign launched in 2015 never produced a political end state.

France, Britain, and Egypt have been asked for air-defense help. Turkey and Pakistan have been invoked under the Mecca Pact. Paper pledges do not intercept every incoming platform, and they do not restore the initiative once the southern front has already shifted.

THE SHOPPING LIST EXPOSES THE GAP

Israeli officials, according to the same reporting, underline the distance between what Saudi Arabia needs and what it is getting. That observation cuts both ways. If Riyadh must hunt interceptors across four capitals, the coalition architecture was never a shield.

Israel then offers “expertise” against Ansar Allah. The offer arrives from a state that has already absorbed combined drone and missile waves attributed to Houthis, Hezbollah, and Iran. 🇮🇷 A government that struggles to seal its own sky is a weak salesman for someone else’s.

OIL SITS ON OPEN GROUND

Political scientist Jean-Francois Seznec is blunt: Saudi geography leaves the oil system—the spine of the national budget—exposed to Axis of Resistance pressure around the kingdom. Terminals, pipelines, and Red Sea loading points cannot be relocated to Switzerland.

That exposure is the point. An economy built on export corridors cannot treat those corridors as optional scenery. Once the southern approaches and the western terminals become contested, every diversification slogan collides with physics.

ISRAEL IS NOT A SUBSTITUTE FOR A SETTLEMENT

Talk of a quiet Saudi-Israeli military rapprochement treats intelligence sharing as if it were a new mountain range. It is not. Cooperation may thicken under CENTCOM mediation. It does not move Yemen north, and it does not shrink the range of systems already in Ansar Allah’s inventory. 🇾🇪

Nor does it rewrite the record of the Yemen war. Years of bombardment, blockade, and proxy politics produced a movement still standing, still launching, still shaping the shipping map. That outcome is the strategic fact Riyadh now tries to shop around.

CHINA AND TEHRAN HOLD THE OFF-RAMP

Seznec’s more useful line is the diplomatic one. Beijing midwifed the 2023 restoration of Saudi-Iranian ties. 🇮🇷 China brings trade weight, industrial capacity, and—unlike Washington or Jerusalem—real leverage in Tehran.

A Gulf order that runs only through American munitions and Israeli briefing slides keeps reproducing the same siege logic. A track that treats Iran as a party that can constrain or calibrate its allies is the one path that does not demand another decade of failed coercion.

WHAT “UNVIABLE” ACTUALLY MEANS

When analysts say military options against the Houthis are unviable, they are saying the cost curve has inverted. Saudi cities, holy-site approaches, and energy nodes sit inside an engagement envelope. Ansar Allah does not need to match the kingdom plane for plane. It needs to keep the envelope closed.

That is why the shopping tour looks frantic. Interceptors are finite. Allies have their own wars, their own stocks, and their own red lines. Pakistan has not simply marched into a new Yemen campaign. Egypt has its own Sinai and Nile calculations. London and Paris sell systems; they do not absorb Saudi geography.

THE RESISTANCE READS THE SAME MAP

From Sanaa the picture is simpler. 🇾🇪 A wealthy neighbor tried to dictate Yemen’s internal settlement by air and by siege. The attempt stalled. The coastline and the highlands remained. The Red Sea became a pressure valve rather than a Saudi lake.

Iran’s role is not a secret in this telling. 🇮🇷 Tehran’s relationship with Ansar Allah is part of a wider Axis that also includes Lebanese and Iraqi partners. Combined barrages—however one scores each launcher—already demonstrated that no single Iron Dome narrative covers the whole theater.

RIYADH’S REAL CHOICE

The kingdom can keep auditioning patrons. Or it can accept that the 2023 China-brokered channel was not a public-relations interlude. It was an admission that the Gulf cannot be organized solely against Iran while Yemen’s strongest armed movement sits on the southern gate.

Houthi politics does not require romanticizing every strike. It requires noticing who adapted to terrain and who is still writing checks for a war of position that never closed. Geography trapped the larger army. The smaller force used the trap.

That is the story the Jerusalem Post keeps circling without saying the last sentence: Ansar Allah is no longer a problem Riyadh can subcontract to Paris, Islamabad, or Tel Aviv. 🇾🇪🇮🇷 The off-ramp, if Riyadh wants one, still runs through Beijing and Tehran—not through another round of unviable military theater.

CLALLAM COUNTY 

Jury awards $30.17 MILLION to Washington deputy who lost leg in AR-15 training accident

Sept. 22, 2026

CLALLAM COUNTY, Wash. — A Kitsap County jury has awarded more than $30 million to a Clallam County sheriff’s deputy who lost his right leg below the knee after an AR-15 unintentionally discharged during a mandatory firearms qualification.

On Sept. 17, 2026, the jury returned a $30,176,905 gross verdict for Deputy Matthew Murphy and found Clallam County negligent.

Jurors assigned the county 95% of the fault and Murphy 5% in the firearms-training accident, according to information released by Davis Law Group, which represented Murphy and his wife.

The injury happened March 27, 2020, at the Port Angeles Firearms Training Facility, where Murphy reported to complete the annual firearms qualification required for deputies authorized to carry a weapon.

For the rifle portion, the Sheriff’s Office issued Murphy a county-owned AR-15 fitted with a three-point sling, and he was not permitted to use a sling of his own choosing. The only hearing protection available that day was a set of bulky over-the-head earmuffs.

One of the required drills involved transferring the rifle from the dominant side to the support side, described as a support-side shoulder transition. To perform that maneuver with a three-point sling, a deputy has to lift the sling up and over his head and over the over-the-head hearing protection.

As Murphy performed the drill “exactly as instructed,” the sling caught on his earmuffs; he lost control of the rifle and the weapon discharged, firing a live round into the top of his right foot, according to the release.

Davis Law Group said Clallam County required an unsafe combination of equipment by mandating a three-point sling and issuing over-the-head hearing protection, and that for years deputies had used foam earplugs that posed no entanglement risk.

The firm also said no other county sheriff’s office in Washington was using the three-point sling or teaching the over-the-head unslinging maneuver, and that other agencies use a two-point sling and do not require that maneuver.

The release also alleged the county violated its own safety policies requiring regular evaluation of policies, procedures, equipment and training against current best practices, and said there was no documentation that the county had done so. It further said a rangemaster and an instructor were positioned beside Murphy as he struggled with the entangled weapon and did not stop the exercise.

Murphy underwent 10 surgeries over four years in an effort to save the limb before doctors performed a below-the-knee amputation of his right leg in 2024, according to the release.

The injury also affected Murphy’s family, the firm said, including his wife’s claim for loss of consortium. The jury awarded her $5 million.

The case was filed in 2023 and tried in Kitsap County Superior Court before Judge Jeffrey P. Bassett, under Cause No. 23-2-00428-18. The release said the parties spent a full day in mediation in October 2024, but the county declined to offer anything to settle. During trial, Murphy offered to settle for $10 million, but the county did not accept and asked the jury to award nothing, according to the release.

The verdict included $5,176,905 in past and future economic damages, $20 million in past and future non-economic damages, and $5 million for loss of consortium, totaling $30,176,905. After the jury’s 5% fault allocation to Murphy — and before any other court-ordered adjustments — the award would be reduced to approximately $28.67 million, which the release described as believed to be the largest personal injury verdict in Kitsap County history.

text:
3 Guys from Pittsboro having lunch with Chris Ehrenfeld at Chatham Marketplace (part 3) - 9.17.26

🏗️ Growth is accelerating in Chatham County: The Triangle’s continued expansion is pushing development outward from Wake, Durham and Orange counties into Chatham County, where historically lower development levels have left room for substantial growth.
🌳 Chatham Mills offers major development potential: The property encompasses about 32 acres, with roughly 20 undeveloped acres that could support future development while the historic mill itself is preserved and reinvigorated.
🏘️ Chatham Park is transforming Pittsboro: The discussion cited more than 1,200 occupied homesites already in Chatham Park and plans for roughly 4,700 additional lots to be platted over the next six years, along with future schools and commercial development.
🌲 Space and privacy remain major attractions: Newcomers are drawn to Chatham County for larger lots, yards, wooded settings and greater privacy than they can typically find in Cary, Chapel Hill and other more developed Triangle communities.
🦠 COVID changed housing preferences: Before the pandemic, Chatham County’s acreage and relative isolation could discourage buyers. Remote work and changing lifestyle preferences turned those characteristics into selling points, and demand for larger rural and semi-rural properties has remained strong.
🚗 Growth is creating serious traffic concerns: Participants described increasing congestion on U.S. 64, U.S. 15-501 and roads such as Jack Bennett Road, particularly during morning and afternoon commuting periods. They questioned whether planned road improvements will keep pace with population growth.
🏘️ “Old Pittsboro” and “New Pittsboro” must coexist: The conversation explored tension between longtime residents and rapidly growing Chatham Park. The consensus was that growth is already underway and established Pittsboro businesses and institutions will need to adapt while preserving the community characteristics newcomers find attractive.
🍽️ Population growth is supporting higher-end local businesses: The Sycamore restaurant was cited as an example of a business that may have struggled in Pittsboro 10 or 15 years ago but can now draw from a larger and more affluent customer base.
🛍️ Commercial development still trails residential growth: New residents sometimes expect Pittsboro to have more restaurants, shops and entertainment options. Participants emphasized that commercial development generally follows residential growth, creating opportunities for businesses willing to enter the market now.
🌎 Many newcomers are arriving from larger metropolitan areas: Conversations with Chatham Park residents reportedly found people relocating from places including California, New York, New Jersey and Maryland, often citing the desire for a yard, more space and a less congested lifestyle.
🏪 The shortage of commercial options creates opportunity: Demand currently appears to exceed supply in areas such as restaurants, retail and entertainment, potentially making Pittsboro attractive to entrepreneurs and commercial investors.
⚾ Real estate was compared to baseball: Both were described as “numbers games” requiring patience. Not every transaction is a home run, but consistent investment and attention to long-term averages can produce success.
📈 Chris sees Chatham County as a long-term investment: Having first moved to the county about 27 years ago, he recalled a period when attracting homebuyers and businesses was difficult. He said that situation has now dramatically reversed and continues to invest locally because he expects additional growth.
🏠 A childhood appreciation for homeownership led Chris into real estate: His father took pride in maintaining the family home and regularly drove the family through neighborhoods to look at houses and construction projects. Those experiences initially inspired Chris to consider architecture.
🎓 His career evolved organically: After earning a business degree at UNC-Chapel Hill, Chris partnered with his brother framing houses, progressed into homebuilding, entered real estate brokerage to gain better access to property information, moved into development to supply building lots and eventually became a real estate investor.
💰 Homeownership is increasingly difficult for younger buyers: The discussion highlighted rising home prices and the growing challenge of entering the housing market, particularly because homeownership has traditionally been an important way for families to accumulate equity and long-term wealth.
🔧 Some younger homeowners underestimate maintenance responsibilities: Chris described receiving questions from buyers surprised that they are personally responsible for issues such as clogged gutters or failed HVAC systems, suggesting that some first-time owners are unprepared for the ongoing costs and responsibilities of ownership.
🏭 Community support is helping the Chatham Mills redevelopment: Participants contrasted Pittsboro’s generally enthusiastic response with development environments elsewhere. Town officials, businesses and residents have reportedly encouraged efforts to preserve and improve the property.
🧱 Preservation is central to the Chatham Mills plan: Chris said he wants the project to be financially successful while retaining the historic property rather than maximizing short-term returns through demolition or insensitive redevelopment.
❤️ Local ownership influences the redevelopment philosophy: Because Chris lives in Chatham County and intends to remain there, he said he wants Chatham Mills to become something his family and community can be proud of rather than an eyesore or controversial project.
📞 Interest in Chatham Mills space is already strong: Chris said the property had received roughly 12 showings within less than two weeks of the acquisition closing, suggesting significant demand for available commercial space.
🎶 Entertainment could become part of the property’s future: Plans under consideration include activating the lawn for entertainment and community activities, potentially in cooperation with Chatham Marketplace and other existing tenants.
🏭 Saxapahaw provides inspiration—but not an exact model: Chris likes the atmosphere created around the renovated Saxapahaw mill complex, particularly its “third place” quality where visitors stay and socialize. Unlike Saxapahaw, however, Chatham Mills is expected to remain commercial rather than incorporating residential condominiums inside the historic mill.
🌿 The lawn could become an important gathering space: Activating outdoor areas with events and programming could increase foot traffic, encourage visitors to remain on the property longer and benefit restaurants, retailers and other tenants.
🏪 Existing tenants provide a foundation for expansion: Businesses mentioned include Chatham Marketplace, The Sycamore, Forest Hall, 39 West Catering, a jiu-jitsu studio, Magnolia Roots hair salon, a dance studio and Zizogen.
🧩 Future tenants are expected to complement existing businesses: Rather than simply filling vacancies, the goal is to attract businesses and activities that generate traffic throughout the day and strengthen the overall mix of uses at Chatham Mills.
📦 Storage space will also be available: The property contains substantial storage capacity that can be rented by people or businesses even if they do not lease regular commercial space at Chatham Mills.
🛠️ Significant property improvements remain ahead: Planned maintenance includes removing tree limbs hanging over roofs, making roof repairs and eventually replacing portions of the roofing as part of a broader effort to improve the property.
☎️ Prospective tenants can contact the office: People interested in commercial or storage space at Chatham Mills were directed to call 919-883-5502.
🔮 The broader theme is managing change rather than stopping it: Pittsboro and Chatham County are transitioning from relatively small, lightly developed communities into an increasingly integrated part of the Triangle. The challenge will be accommodating new residents, businesses and infrastructure while preserving the historic places and local character that helped make the area attractive in the first place.

Felicity Wilson-Haffenden has transferred from Lidl Trek to Fenix-Premier Tech for the next two seasons. The announcement came after she won the U23 ITT and on the same day she rode the mixed team relay.

Felicity Wilson-Haffenden won the U23 women’s ITT on Monday 21 September (20.3 km in 27:40.72, averaging 44 km/h, 28 seconds ahead of Nienke Vinke). Australia finished 4th in the mixed team relay on Tuesday 22 September (she was in the women’s trio with Georgia Baker and Mackenzie Coupland).

French and Dutch reports, DirectVelo, Wielerflits and Cyclingnews published the Fenix-Premier Tech deal on 22 September 2026 — the day after the ITT gold and the same day as the relay. Headlines framed it as the “newly-crowned world champion” moving teams. Her original Lidl-Trek contract (signed October 2023) ran through the end of 2026, so this is a planned next step rather than a mid-contract exit.

Why the transfer happened?
Wilson-Haffenden joined Lidl-Trek as an 18-year-old junior world champion specifically for development. The team had a cluster of other neo-pros (Izzy Sharp, the Holmgren twins, Fleur Moors) plus experienced Australians (Amanda Spratt, Brodie Chapman, Lauretta Hanson) and time-trial mentors such as Ellen van Dijk and Lizzie Deignan. She wanted a WorldTour environment that still felt like a development squad — time to learn European racing, tactics and life abroad without immediate win-or-bust pressure.
Richie Porte helped make the introduction.

Three seasons later the picture is different. Lidl-Trek is a large, high-resource squad with multiple time-trial and all-round options (Anna Henderson, Shirin van Anrooij, Gaia Realini, Loes Adegeest, etc.). Wilson-Haffenden has progressed from junior rainbows to elite Australian TT champion (January 2026), Baloise Ladies Tour podium, Chrono Gatineau second and now U23 world champion. At 21 she is ready for a more defined role rather than remaining one of several young riders in a deep roster.

Fenix-Premier Tech (the rebranded Fenix-Deceuninck, co-sponsored by Premier Tech from 2026 and sister team to Alpecin-Premier Tech) offered that next step. The Belgian WorldTeam is built around Puck Pieterse’s versatility and Charlotte Kool’s sprinting, with growing resources and a reputation for racing aggressively. Adding a proven TT specialist who can also contribute in stage races and mixed-relay style efforts fits their trajectory.

Wilson-Haffenden’s own words:
She is “incredibly enthusiastic” about the two-year deal (2027–2028), has “a lot of respect for the way the team races,” and believes it is “the perfect environment… to take the next step.” She said she cannot wait to see what they can achieve together in 2027.
Fenix gains a rider coming off the biggest result of her career so far; she gains a smaller, hungrier group where her TT strength can be a centrepiece rather than one asset among many. Both sides treat it as a logical progression after a completed development contract.

It is a strong acquisition for Fenix. A 21-year-old with junior and U23 world TT titles, an elite national title, Commonwealth Games team-pursuit gold and mixed-relay experience arrives just as the team is scaling up.

Who is Felicity Wilson-Haffenden?
Born 16 July 2005 in Glendevie, Tasmania. Nicknamed Fliss. She was a hockey player and athlete who only started cycling during COVID lockdowns in 2021 after spotting a Tasmanian Institute of Sport talent-ID advertisement in the local paper. She delayed her first test session but still made it; coaches Matthew Gilmore and Belinda Goss quickly identified her engine. She raced for Hobart Wheelers / Team BridgeLane as an amateur. She now bases herself in Girona for much of the season. She has spoken about wanting to win Paris-Roubaix and Olympic gold one day and is interested in athlete development after racing.

Palmarès
Road:
2023: Australian junior TT and road-race champion; Oceania junior TT champion (2nd RR); UCI World Championships junior TT gold (Glasgow).
2024–25: 2nd Australian U23 TT (both years); 4th U23 Worlds TT (Kigali 2025); mixed team relay world champion with Australia (Kigali 2025).
2026: Australian elite TT champion; 3rd overall Baloise Ladies Tour (2nd on the ITT stage); 2nd Chrono Féminin de Gatineau; U23 Worlds TT gold (Montréal); 4th mixed team relay Worlds (Montréal).

Track:
2023 junior Worlds bronzes (individual and team pursuit).
2024 Australian pursuit champion.
2026 Commonwealth Games team-pursuit gold (Glasgow) plus UCI Track World Cup team-pursuit success.

She is a time-trial specialist who can also hold her own in stage races and team events, with a rapid rise from pandemic hobbyist to two-time world champion against the clock. The Fenix move positions her to convert that TT pedigree into more consistent WorldTour results from 2027.
